analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using noncompete agreements that block workers from taking new jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was assigned to, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to make workers sign noncompete agreements — contracts that bar an employee from working for a competitor or in the same field for months or years after leaving a job. The Department of Labor could fine violators up to $5,000 per worker per week, and workers could sue for damages and attorney fees. Employers could still require workers not to share trade secrets.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30 million American workers who, by widely cited estimates, are covered by a noncompete agreement — including low-wage workers in fields like fast food, hair care, and telemarketing, not just executives. Workers could change jobs freely, negotiate raises using outside offers, and start competing businesses without lawsuits.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from entering into, enforcing, or threatening to enforce a covenant not to compete with any employee covered by the bill [S3] [S2].
Requires employers to post a notice of the noncompete prohibition at the workplace [S3].
Directs the Department of Labor to investigate complaints and impose civil fines of up to $5,000 per aggrieved employee per week of violation [S3] [S2].
Gives aggrieved employees a right to sue in federal court for actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees if they prevail [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompetes to hold onto trained workers and suppress their wages would lose that tool, and would face fines up to $5,000 per worker per week plus damage suits. Businesses that rely on noncompetes to protect investments in training would bear the cost if workers leave with that training.

drawbacks.text: Some employers argue noncompetes protect investments in training and trade secrets; the bill keeps trade-secret agreements but removes a legal tool some firms use to keep competitors from poaching trained staff [S3].
The bill applies only to new agreements entered into after enactment and leaves state noncompete laws untouched for agreements outside its commerce coverage, so existing contracts would stand [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is broad: research cited in the wider noncompete debate finds such agreements depress wages and reduce job mobility, especially for lower-paid workers. The cost falls on firms that use the agreements to retain trained staff, though the bill preserves trade-secret protection, which addresses the most common legitimate employer concern. The main design limit is that it only reaches new agreements.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the Workforce Mobility Act of 2018 in the Senate on April 26, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5] [S1].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was recorded, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use noncompete agreements kept a legal tool for restricting workers' job options, because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no vote record shows how the parties lined up; its three sponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompete agreements (staffing firms, chains, professional-services firms)
industries.note: The bill would take away their ability to restrict workers from joining competitors and expose violators to fines of up to $5,000 per worker per week and civil suits. Restricting job mobility lets such employers hold wages down.

industries.industry: Workers and small businesses competing for talent
industries.note: Workers could change jobs or start businesses without litigation risk, and small firms could hire from larger rivals more freely.
